definition: A visual examination of a home's systems and condition by a qualified inspector, usually ordered by the buyer.
An inspection a seller orders before listing to find problems early. Anything found becomes known to the seller and must be disclosed.
The buyer's last look at the property before closing to confirm its condition and agreed repairs.
A sale where the seller won't make repairs. It doesn't excuse hiding known defects.
A federal rule for housing built before 1978: sellers and landlords must disclose known lead hazards, give the EPA pamphlet, and buyers get a 10-day chance to test.
A colorless, odorless radioactive gas from the natural decay of uranium in soil. A leading cause of lung cancer. Detected by testing.
A mineral fiber once used in insulation, flooring and siding. Dangerous when friable (crumbling) and its fibers are inhaled.
Sealing hazardous material, like asbestos, in place instead of removing it.
Fungal growth caused by moisture. Can cause health problems and signals a water issue.
A buried tank for fuel or chemicals. Leaks can contaminate soil and groundwater.
A chemical once used in foam insulation and some building products that can release irritating gas.
A colorless, odorless gas from incomplete burning of fuel, from faulty furnaces or water heaters. Detectors warn of it.
A property with a non-physical issue, like a death or crime, that may affect buyers' feelings. Disclosure rules vary by state.
A form, required in many states, where the seller reports known conditions of the property.
Something a licensee notices, like a water stain or crack, that suggests a possible problem and should be disclosed and investigated.
Government's power to regulate property to protect public health, safety and welfare, through zoning, building codes and similar rules. No compensation is owed.
Government's power to take private property for public use, with just compensation.
The legal process the government uses to exercise eminent domain.
Government's power to tax property. Unpaid taxes become a lien.
A tax on properties that benefit from a specific public improvement, like new sidewalks.
Property passing to the state when an owner dies with no will and no heirs.
A tax based on value, like property tax.
An owner's lawsuit to force the government to pay when its action has effectively taken the property's value.
A community's long-range plan for land use, growth and services. Zoning carries it out.
Local laws dividing land into zones and setting permitted uses, density, heights and setbacks.
Permission to deviate from zoning requirements, like a setback, because strict compliance causes hardship.
A use that was legal before a zoning change and may continue, often with limits. Also called grandfathered.
Permission for a use allowed in a zone only with approval and conditions, like a church in a residential zone.
Rezoning a single parcel differently from its surroundings for one owner's benefit. Often invalid.
Construction standards for safety and quality, enforced through permits and inspections.
A local government document stating a building complies with codes and may be occupied.
The minimum distance a building must be from property lines.
Land, like a park, separating incompatible uses, such as industrial and residential.
Federal law on cleaning up hazardous waste sites. Current and past owners can be liable for cleanup, even if they didn't cause the contamination.
A review of a property's history and records for likely contamination, used to support the innocent landowner defense.
Land saturated with water for part of the year. Filling them generally requires a federal permit under the Clean Water Act.
An area FEMA maps as having a 1% annual chance of flooding. Federally backed loans there require flood insurance.
Covenants, conditions and restrictions: private rules recorded for a subdivision or community.
A private limit on use written in a deed, like a height limit.
A private promise limiting use. Breaking it is usually remedied by an injunction or damages.
A restriction whose violation can cause the owner to lose title. A harsher remedy than a covenant.
A court order requiring someone to stop doing something, like violating a deed restriction.
An association of owners that enforces CC&Rs, maintains common areas, and collects assessments.
